extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science (physicists, chemists, natural philosophers) learning laboratory and experimental method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for designing, controlling, and interpreting experiments in the physical and natural sciences, focusing on control of variables, detection/exclusion of interfering agents, validation, and cautious interpretation of negative results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary only one circumstance at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most requisite precautions in experimentation is to vary only one circumstance at a time, and to maintain all other circumstances rigidly unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two reasons: (1) if two conditions are varied simultaneously and an effect is found, one cannot tell which condition caused it or whether both jointly caused it; (2) if no effect ensues, one cannot safely conclude either is indifferent because one may have neutralised the other's effect. Symbolic example: AB + Ab identical with A only if B is truly indifferent. Example pitfalls: using a burning candle to exhaust oxygen also adds carbonic acid, confounding the result. Always design experiments so only one antecedent differs between cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification of experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: In performing experiments, it is a necessary principle that they be simplified as much as possible, and that every circumstance capable of rendering their results complicated be carefully removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolate bodies and reduce to utmost simplicity to bring each property separately into action. Historical advice from Lavoisier and Cuvier: avoid using complex mixtures (e.g., atmospheric air) when a purer medium is needed. Use apparatus that minimizes extraneous effects (e.g., electro-magnets versus heavy permanent magnets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controllable apparatus to demonstrate cause-and-effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer apparatus whose action can be rapidly and cleanly controlled, reversed, or stopped so that dependence of cause and effect can be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the electro-magnet can be switched on/off to show that light ceases and reappears with the current, demonstrating perfect dependence. Controllable devices avoid disturbing the rest of the apparatus (less shaking, currents, temperature changes). Use reversible controls to show immediate causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question and test assumed indifferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept assumed indifferences of circumstances without testing their real existence by appropriate experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical caution: Newton assumed many things were indifferent (e.g., prism matter) and erred; Faraday disproved beliefs (e.g., that water was essential for electrolysis). When unexplained discrepancies arise, revisit assumptions of independence and test them explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When isolation is impossible, use the Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single circumstance cannot be isolated experimentally, collect many instances where the circumstance is present with the result and many where its absence coincides with the absence of the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparative method (agreement and difference) supports probable induction. Example: to investigate double refraction, compare many substances having the property and note common features (e.g., crystallinity). Complement with experiments that change elasticity (compressing glass) when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary conditions widely and test extreme/unusual states
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment to judge the behaviour of substances under conditions widely different from ordinary terrestrial conditions (temperature, pressure, vacuum, gravity, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extreme apparatus and methods—electric arc for high temperatures, Faraday's freezing mixtures for very low temperatures, air-pumps and vacua to vary pressure, neutral buoyancy to mitigate gravity—to learn how laws and properties extrapolate beyond everyday experience. Be cautious when extrapolating quantitative laws far from observed conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of unsuspected interfering conditions; detect and exclude impurities
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to the possible presence of substances or powers not noticed that may influence results; take measures to detect and exclude them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: traces of gold/silver in samples, common salt in the air affecting spectrum analysis, impurities in reagents. Procedures: change vessel materials (glass vs agate vs gold), use distilled water, avoid contact with fingers, run experiments under exhausted receivers. Systematically vary conditions to locate sources of interference (Davy's method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally disturb apparatus and repeat under varied conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: For important experiments, repeat trials in many varied conditions and intentionally disturb the apparatus to try to reveal weak points or accidental regularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If results are more regular than expected, suspect apparatus peculiarity. Vary small components (balls, rods, suspension) and observe effects of visitors, storms, etc. Purposefully seek accidental failures to ensure robustness (Baily's precautions in measuring Earth's density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind or test experiments (controls and blanks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform blind experiments or control trials to check whether the supposed cause is necessary for the observed effect—i.e., test whether the effect appears in the absence of the suspected cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemists' practice: run a blank (absence of suspected substance) to verify no spurious signal (e.g., arsenic from impurities in zinc/acid). A blind trial is essential, not optional; Faraday's test of apparatus magnetism (testing apparatus alone) is cited as a blind experiment. Use controls whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and validation by known quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Test the accuracy of a method by introducing known amounts of the substance or force to be detected and by assaying mixtures of known composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical processes should be validated against standards and known mixtures (e.g., gold assay tested on alloys of known composition). For new quantitative methods, perform spiked samples to verify recovery and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret negative results with caution; consider instrument sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative experimental results should be interpreted cautiously because an effect may exist at a magnitude too small for current instruments or masked by larger effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot by a single experiment prove non-existence. Always consider detection limits and whether greater measurement delicacy could reveal the effect (example: we cannot safely affirm the moon has no atmosphere at all; only put bounds on its density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure apparatus is sufficiently perfect and detect mechanical imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical imperfections or insufficiencies in apparatus can produce false negatives or misleading results; verify the apparatus is adequate to the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early air-pumps and vacuum apparatus produced erroneous conclusions (e.g., sound in imperfect vacua). Test and improve apparatus performance before drawing strong inferences; otherwise negative or positive findings may reflect apparatus limits rather than nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design comparative experiments to separate entwined variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When two properties always vary together (e.g., colour and internal structure), design experiments that vary one while holding the other constant to identify the relevant factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Leslie's observation that changing colour also changed internal structure; for dew experiments expose same material polished or varnished to vary surface independently, or expose different substances with the same surface. Take care not to change internal structure when altering superficial properties.
